title: What time, what day
goal: Tell the time using both number systems at once, say days and dates, make plans, and use 부터 … 까지 for time spans.
bekal: read hours with native Korean numbers and minutes with Sino-Korean numbers
name the seven days of the week
read dates from largest to smallest
use 에 for time and know when to leave it out
make a simple plan with 언제 and 몇 시에

dialogs.title: 대화 — Making plans
dialogs.intro: Suji asks Ani to study together. Notice how, within a single time expression, both number systems work side by side without getting in each other's way.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ani, what time does your class finish today?
lines.literal: Ani — Ms., today — what — hour-at — class — subject — finish?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Let's study together. How about four thirty?
lines.literal: together — study. four — hour — half-at — how-is-it?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Let's meet in front of the library. The library is open from nine to ten.
lines.literal: library — front-at — meet. library — as-for — nine — hour-from — ten — hour-until — open.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Got it. By the way, what day is tomorrow?
lines.literal: understood. by-the-way, tomorrow — as-for — what — day — is?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Tomorrow is Friday. The day after is Saturday.
lines.literal: tomorrow — as-for — Friday — is. day-after-tomorrow — as-for — Saturday — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Is there an exam on Saturday?

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: No, the exam is next Monday. June fifteenth.
lines.literal: no, exam — as-for — next — week — Monday — is. June — fifteenth-day — is.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: There's still time. What a relief.
lines.literal: still — time — subject — exists. relief — is.

notes: **One time expression uses both number systems.** 네 시 십 분 = ten past four. **네** is native Korean for the hour, **십** is Sino-Korean for the minutes. It's not chaos: hours are counted as an *amount*, minutes are read as a *figure*. Once you accept that, it never confuses you again.

**반 means half, and it goes after 시.** 네 시 반 = four thirty, half past four. Korean counts from the hour that has **already passed**, just like English, so there's no trap here — simply "four hour half".

**The time particle 에 is used for hours, days and dates — but not for every time word.** 세 시**에**, 월요일**에**, 유월**에** all take 에. But **오늘, 내일, 어제, 지금, 언제, 매일** never do — just as English says "at three" but never "at today". 오늘에 만나요 is wrong; it's 오늘 만나요.
**부터 … 까지 for time, 에서 … 까지 for place.** 아홉 시**부터** 열 시**까지** (from nine to ten); 집**에서** 학교**까지** (from home to school). An easy pair to mix up, and a mix-up sounds wrong immediately.
**무슨 요일이에요? is the standard way to ask the day.** Note that 무슨 ("what") is used before a noun, while 뭐 stands alone. 무슨 책이에요? (what book?) but 이거 뭐예요? (what's this?).

**알겠어요 means "I see" or "okay, got it".** It looks like a future/past form of 알다 (to know) but means "understood" right now. Its opposite is 모르겠어요 ("I'm not sure"), far gentler than 몰라요 ("I don't know"), which can sound curt.
**어때요? is the Swiss Army knife of conversation.** It means "how about it?", used to suggest (네 시 반에 어때요?), ask an opinion (이거 어때요?), and ask how things are (한국 생활 어때요?). One word, three jobs.
**이따가 and 나중에 both mean "later".** 이따가 means later **today**, within hours. 나중에 means some vague later — next week, or never. Saying 나중에 봐요 to someone commits nobody to anything.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Hours use **native Korean numbers + 시**. Minutes use **Sino-Korean numbers + 분**. No exceptions.
after: **오전 and 오후 go in front**, not behind like a.m. and p.m.: 오전 아홉 시 (9 a.m.), 오후 세 시 (3 p.m.). For evening and night, use 저녁 or 밤: 밤 열 시.
Korean uses morning/afternoon markers less than English uses a.m./p.m., since the 24-hour clock is common in written schedules. In conversation, context is usually enough.

grammars.title: Days and dates
body: The seven days follow one pattern: an element of nature + 요일. Dates use Sino-Korean numbers throughout.
after: **Dates go from largest to smallest: year – month – day.** 2026년 6월 15일 = June 15, 2026. The same applies to addresses: country, city, street, number.

⚠️ **Two months break the pattern.** June should be 육월 but is written and read **유월**; October should be 십월 but becomes **시월**. Purely for ease of pronunciation. Learn these two separately — every other month follows number + 월.

blocks.title: 시 vs. 시간
items: **시** names a point in time: 세 시 = three o'clock.
**시간** names a duration: 세 시간 = three hours.
세 시에 만나요 = meet at three. 세 시간 공부해요 = study for three hours. One syllable apart, worlds apart in meaning.
The same holds for 분: 십 분 can mean "ten past" or "ten minutes long" — here context comes to the rescue.
